catalog_quote: Second, it seems unlikely that Yali has stressed syllables, where stress would then be signaled at the word level by other cues than f0. The duration measures in this study provide a first coarse indication that there are no stress differences between final and non-final syllables at the word level (i.e. both in non-final phrase positions; nf, nn). ... it seems that Yali can be tentatively categorised as a non-stress-accent language with only post-lexical pitch (as Bengali; Table 1). ... It is therefore more plausible that Yali has a word-level (pitch) accent system rather than word stress. ... To conclude, this study has shown that Apahapsili Yali makes use of word-final rising f0 contours on content words and that these can be overwritten by phrase-level boundary tones. [p. 21] At the word-level, final syllables are regularly found with a high or rising f0 movement, whereas non-final syllables show lower-level movements ... Both suffixes and enclitics are treated as word-final syllables for the purposes of placing the word-final rise: there are usually rises on suffixed or cliticized syllables and there never are rises on stem-final syllables when followed by a suffix or a clitic. [p. 7]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level prominence in (Apahapsili) Yali is a high/rising f0 target on the FINAL syllable of the phonological word; suffixes and enclitics count as part of the word, so the rise lands on the suffix/clitic syllable, never on the stem-final syllable before it (p. 7). The rise is clearest on phrase-medial words and is overridden phrase-finally by boundary tones (falls in statements). Duration shows no final vs non-final difference beyond phrase-final lengthening, so the authors tentatively conclude there is no word stress and classify Yali as a non-stress-accent language with a word-final, probably post-lexical, pitch accent; no lexical f0 contrasts are attested. For a position catalog: fixed word-final prominence, cued by f0 only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; non-final syllables show lower/falling f0 (declination), with anticipatory lows on penults.
new_statements.exceptions: Phrase-final words: word-final rise replaced by boundary fall (or discourse-continuation rise); free grammatical function words (e.g. fam 'on/in') do not attract the rise, unlike suffixes/enclitics; six non-final-word final syllables with low falls were all creaky-voiced; the final rise is a strong trend (61% rises, 84% high-register contours on nf syllables) rather than exceptionless.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word / clitic group in connected spontaneous speech (not citation forms); authors leave open whether the rise belongs to the phonological word, clitic group or an accentual phrase. Study explicitly tentative ('first exploration'); whether word stress is truly absent is left for future work (vowel quality, spectral tilt untested).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Apahapsili Yali (Glottolog dialect apah1238; DoReCo 'Yali (Apahapsili)'), which Glottolog/Ethnologue subsume under Pass Valley Yali [pass1247, iso yac] together with Landikma, Pass Valley proper and (per Fahner/Riesberg) Abenaho. The Riesberg 2021 sketch examined is attached to an Angguruk Yali dictionary (angg1239, iso yli) but uses Apahapsili examples; it is silent on stress either way.

tone_statements.quote: The Angguruk dictionary ... as well as the other sources on Dani languages make no reference to lexical items that can be distinguished solely by f0, which for now we take as a reason to exclude the option of classifying Yali as a language with lexically contrastive tone ... It seems, therefore, that f0 might play a role at the word-level in Yali prosody such that the final syllables of words have a high tonal target. ... the only acoustic evidence for Yali so far concerns f0. It is therefore more plausible that Yali has a word-level (pitch) accent system rather than word stress.

sources.note: Instrumental study of Apahapsili Yali spontaneous speech (30 speakers): word-final syllables (suffixes and enclitics count as word-final) carry a high/rising f0 target, clearest phrase-medially and overridden by phrase-final boundary falls; duration gives no evidence of stress, so the authors tentatively conclude Yali has no word stress but a word-final (probably post-lexical) pitch accent; no lexical f0 contrasts attested (pp. 7-9, 19-21).

sources.note: Ch.2 'Prosodic Phrasing' (pp.32-58) gives the first phonological (AM) analysis of Yali prosody: IUs show a regular L H alternation with an H target on every word-final syllable (shifting onto suffixes/enclitics), analysed as a (L+)H right-edge tone of an Accentual Phrase whose minimal domain is the phonological word; LH may reduce to level H on short/function words; IU-final L% boundary tone (finality) replaces the last AP's H, continuative IUs end on the AP H, sometimes raised; sec. 2.4.1 argues against word stress (no duration cue, not contrastive, domain can exceed the word), sec. 2.4.2 fi…

tone.quote: I analyse IUs in Yali as being structured into APs, which are marked by a (L+)H tone on their right edge. APs, in my understanding, are small prosodic constituents, usually of the size of one phonological word. ... From my data, at the current stage of analysis, I do not have any reason for assuming word stress in Yali. However, Yali does have a rather regularly word-final pitch rise ... the word-final pitch movement is not lexically contrastive, but occurs completely regularly with just any (type of) word. ... I describe this pitch rise as an edge tone marking the right boundary of the AP in Yali ... At least for Yali, there is no substantive evidence for lexical pitch contours

tone.quote: In Yali as well as in Dani, the accent is realized by "upgliding pitch and/or increased loudness" (49). Polysyllabic words which are monomorphemic have one word accent, resting on the final syllable. The same is the case with words which in terms of morphology contain a suffix (50). In the morphology of compound and composite verbs, however, we frequently meet forms where the accent is not on the final syllable of the form, but on the final syllable of its first component; sometimes this primary word accent is accompanied by a secondary accent on the word-final syllable (51).
